text: The EC-155 comes with two coffee filters and a measuring spoon; the smaller filter one is for one shot of espresso and the second filter is for two shots (see user manual at, e.g., here). Fill the smaller (or larger) filter with one (or two) loosely filled spoons and press lightly using the disc that is attached to the machine. A single shot is considered to be about 30 mL (1 US fluid ounce) but this is really a matter of taste and personal preferences. For a single shot in a standard size espresso cup, I would suggest starting with filling half a cup and then adjusting the amount of coffee that you pour to accommodate your taste (and need for caffeine...).

A load of coffee grounds can only be brewed once. After one extraction, the coffee oils and pleasant flavors are depleted; running more water through the same puck produces weak, overly bitter, and astringent liquid. How many shots you yield from that single brew depends on which filter basket you insert into the portafilter: --- Shot Volume and Basket Yield | Basket | Coffee Dose | Yield | Volume (with crema) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Single Basket (shallow) | ~7 g (1 level scoop) | 1 Single Shot | ~30 ml (1 fl oz) | | Double Basket (deep) | ~12–14 g (2 level scoops) | 1 Double Shot (or 2 singles) | ~60 ml (2 fl oz) | If you use the double basket, the portafilter has two spouts at the bottom. You can place one cup underneath to catch a double shot (~60 ml), or place two espresso cups side by side to catch two single shots (~30 ml each) at the same time. --- Operating the Manual Dial on the EC-155 The De’Longhi EC-155 is a manual machine, meaning water will keep pumping until you turn the knob off: Start the brew: Turn the front selector knob to the coffee/cup icon. Watch the output: Stop at ~30 ml for a single basket (takes ~20–25 seconds). Stop at ~60 ml for a double basket (takes ~25–30 seconds). Stop the brew: Turn the knob back to the center "ON" position as soon as the target volume is reached or the flow turns pale yellow and watery ("blonding"). Empty the puck: Discard the spent coffee puck before packing fresh grounds for your next shot.

Keeping Food Fresh by Janet Bailey says: Keep stored eggs covered. Eggs readily absorb odors from, and lose moisture to, the air circulating in the refrigerator. The best container for them is the carton you bought them in. Don't use the open egg racks in the door of the refrigerator. The rack is too warm and unprotected. Store eggs with their broad, rounded ends up. This position helps the chalaza keep the yolk centered in the white, away from the air pocket where it might encounter unfriendly bacteria. The rounded end of the egg is also less likely to break when accidentally bumped. Don't wash eggs before you store them. If they have been coated in oil, you would be washing away that valuable protection.

You’re actually doing the right thing by keeping eggs in their original carton! For most households, the original carton is the best place to store eggs in the refrigerator, and that little open egg tray is largely a convenience accessory rather than a better storage solution. The best way to store eggs 1\. Keep them in their original carton The carton protects eggs from bumps, absorbs some moisture, and helps prevent them from picking up odors from foods such as onions, cheese, and leftovers. It also keeps the expiration or best-before date handy. 2\. Put them on an interior shelf The back or middle of a refrigerator shelf is generally better than the door because the temperature is more stable. Keep the refrigerator at 4°C (40°F) or below. 3\. Keep the pointed ends down This helps keep the yolks more centered and is a sensible way to position eggs, although it matters much less for food safety than maintaining a consistently cold temperature. Why the refrigerator's open egg tray isn't ideal More exposure to odors: Eggs have porous shells and can absorb odors. Less protection: The carton provides cushioning against accidental knocks and cracks. More temperature fluctuation: If the tray is on the door, eggs experience frequent warming whenever the refrigerator opens. Less information: You lose the original date and packaging information when transferring eggs to the tray. The open tray isn't inherently unsafe, though. If you prefer it, you can use it as long as the eggs are kept cold, clean, and protected from contamination. One important detail: washing eggs Egg-storage advice differs by country. In the United States, commercially sold eggs are washed and sanitized, so refrigeration is essential. In many European countries, eggs are generally not washed before sale, and storage practices differ. Follow the advice on your egg packaging and your local food-safety guidance. For typical U.S. refrigerated eggs, a useful rule is to use them within 3–5 weeks of purchase, provided they have been continuously refrigerated. Don't rely on the smell test alone to establish safety. My recommendation: Keep the carton, put it on an interior shelf, and set the refrigerator to 4°C or below. Simple, inexpensive, and generally the best approach.

Well, brown rice is brown rice: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_rice That's not a particularly fast-cooking meal, though; brown rice can take up to 50min to cook fully. It is very nutritious, though. I have no idea what your anonymous tipster meant by "brown noodles". I would help if you actually quoted her or gave us a name. The modernist food periodical Lucky Peach (http://www.mcsweeneys.net/luckypeach) included a long article on how to spruce up instant ramen; maybe you should check it out.

What it is Brown rice is whole-grain rice with the bran and germ still on. White rice has them milled off. It's chewier, nuttier, and has more fiber. "Brown noodles" probably means whole-wheat noodles or pasta, or possibly soba (buckwheat) or brown rice noodles. Any of these works. Whole-wheat spaghetti is the easiest to find. What to add Protein: chicken thighs or breast, eggs, tofu, ground turkey, canned tuna, or canned beans (the cheapest and fastest). Vegetables: frozen mixed vegetables are the best budget option. Fresh broccoli, spinach, carrots, bell pepper, cabbage, and onion also work. Flavor: soy sauce, garlic, a little oil, and pepper or chili are enough. How to cook it Rice: Rinse 1 cup of brown rice. Add about 2 cups of water and boil, then cover and simmer on low for 40 to 45 minutes. A rice cooker is easier, and most have a brown rice setting. Cook a big batch on Sunday and refrigerate or freeze portions. Reheating takes about 2 minutes, which is the real time-saver. Noodles: Boil according to the package, usually 8 to 12 minutes. Protein and vegetables: Heat a pan with a little oil. Cook bite-sized pieces of chicken or tofu for 5 to 7 minutes until done (chicken to 165°F / 74°C inside). Add the vegetables for 3 to 5 minutes, using frozen ones straight from the bag. Combine: Add the rice or noodles and a splash of soy sauce and garlic, stir 1 to 2 minutes, and eat. If you tell me what kitchen equipment you'll have (rice cooker, microwave, stove), I can tailor this.

There are several things in general that you can do to increase the speed at which food cools down, but two of the most effective are: Increase the surface area. Spread it in a wide, shallow pan, like a sheet pan, rather than a deep pot. This will allow more cooling. Use an ice water bath. Place the container with the food into an ice water bath, being careful not to spill the water into the food. Using a zip style bag to hold the food before putting it into the bath also can help. A variation of this, especially for hot stocks or stews, is to freeze water in clean water bottles or zip bags, and place those into the food in addition to the ice bath. For a pilaf, the first method should work very well. You can also bring physics to the party: Convection is far more powerful at heat transfer than conduction. A fan for air cooling will help, or running water for water for water cooling will also help, but these are not always practical in kitchen.

Cooling a Hot Pot Safely Before Refrigerating The Short Answer No, the "wake up in a few hours to put it in the fridge" plan is not safe. Leaving a large pot of meat-and-rice at room temperature for several hours is a classic food-safety risk. The "danger zone" is 4°C to 60°C (40°F–140°F), and bacteria can multiply rapidly in that range. The FDA/USDA guidance is that perishable food should not sit in the danger zone for more than 2 hours total (1 hour if the ambient temperature is above 32°C/90°F). A big, full pot of plof — dense rice, chicken, carrots, onions — will hold heat for a long time. The center may still be well above 60°C for an hour or more, then spend hours in the danger zone. Waking up "a few hours" later is likely 3–5+ hours of unsafe cooling. That's a risk for food poisoning (Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus in rice, Clostridium perfringens in meat/stew — all classic for exactly this kind of dish). Does the meat matter? Yes, somewhat — but rice is actually a major culprit too. Meat (chicken): high-protein, high-moisture — ideal for bacterial growth (Salmonella, Campylobacter, C. perfringens). Cooked rice: Bacillus cereus spores survive cooking and germinate at room temperature; reheated rice is one of the most common causes of food poisoning worldwide. This is a well-documented risk. The combination (meat + rice + moist vegetables) is basically a perfect bacterial incubator. So even a vegetarian plof would be risky, but the meat adds another layer of concern. Either way, the gradual-cooling plan is not safe. Better techniques to cool it fast The goal: get from cooking temperature to ≤4°C (40°F) within 2 hours, without dumping a screaming-hot pot into the fridge. 1. Divide and conquer (most effective) Split the plof into several shallow containers (depth ≤5 cm / 2 inches). Surface area-to-volume ratio is everything. A wide, shallow container cools dramatically faster than a deep pot. Portion into meal-sized containers you'll actually refrigerate/freeze. 2. Use an ice bath (rapid cooling) Put the pot (or the divided containers) into a larger bowl/sink of ice water, stirring the food occasionally. This is the standard restaurant method. It can bring food down fast without heating your fridge. 3. Stir and spread Stirring releases heat from the center. Spreading food thin in a tray helps a lot. Don't cover tightly while hot — trapping steam slows cooling. (Cover once it's cooled to fridge temp, or use a loose lid/paper towel.) 4. Pre-chill the containers Put the empty containers in the fridge/freezer beforehand so they don't insulate the food. 5. The fridge is fine if the food is portioned The reason you don't want to put a whole hot pot in the fridge is correct: it warms the fridge and risks other food. But small, shallow, loosely covered containers of hot-ish food are fine to put in the fridge — modern fridges recover quickly. Many food-safety authorities actually recommend refrigerating promptly rather than leaving it out. 6. Don't rely on "it'll be fine" for a few hours If you genuinely can't cool it properly tonight, the safer fallback is: keep it hot (≥60°C) until morning (e.g., on a low simmer/stovetop or in a slow cooker) — hot-holding is safe, gradual cooling is not. Or cool it in an ice bath now for 30–45 minutes, then portion and refrigerate before bed. Practical plan for tonight Now: portion the plof into several shallow containers. Ice bath the containers (or the pot) for ~30–45 min, stirring occasionally, until they're lukewarm/cool to the touch. Refrigerate the shallow containers (loosely covered, or cover after they've stopped steaming). Skip the timer-wake-up plan — it's the riskiest option. Bottom line Gradual cooling overnight = not safe, especially for meat + rice. The meat matters, but rice alone is already a significant risk. Divide into shallow containers + ice bath + refrigerate promptly is the safe, fridge-friendly method. Your instinct about not putting a whole hot pot in the fridge is right — but the solution is portioning, not leaving it out for hours. Enjoy the plof — just get it cold fast! 🍲

I don't know of anything for mustard akin to the chilli 'cures' such as yoghurt, milk, etc but as a general rule, vinegar knocks back the heat of mustard, water emphasises it. Additionally, water-based will naturally lose its heat much faster than vinegar-based - which is why you generally make up mustard powder only 15 mins or so before you use it. Pure water/mustard mix will have noticeably lost its edge after only a day. It might depend on how, or if, your mustard is preserved initially. If it was water-based then canned, then knocking it back with vinegar & a milder mustard powder would change the flavour profile but may also change its shelf-life. If it's vinegar-based initially, then I think your only option is to somehow dilute it. I would go with a milder home-made mustard. It may depend on where in the world you live as to the availability of mustard powders. Here in the UK the only ubiquitous one is an English, Coleman's, which will certainly not reduce the burn at all & may actually increase it. In general, darker colour mustards are milder, lighter are hotter. 'Fake' ready-made mustards like McDonald's use all kinds of fillers, bulkers & colourings to make a yellow 'mustard' with almost no taste of mustard at all, so don't let that fool you. If you don't mind changing the flavour profile completely, then will mix with mayo - which, in effect, just dilutes the mustard. Honey will sweeten it & dilute somewhat. Sweet will mask the hot to an extent.

That intense, sinuses-clearing rush comes from allyl isothiocyanate, the exact same compound found in wasabi and horseradish. Unlike chili's capsaicin (which binds to heat sensors on the tongue), isothiocyanates are volatile compounds that vaporize and shoot up through the back of your throat straight into your nasal passages. Because isothiocyanates are heat-sensitive and volatile, you have two primary ways to tame the jar without ruining the flavor or silky texture: blending in complementary bases or harnessing time and gentle heat. --- Method 1: The Best Mix-Ins (Dilution & Fat Coating) Fat coats the palate and slows the release of volatile vapors, while mild sweet or acid elements balance out mustard's sharp profile. Mix these in small batches rather than doctoring the entire jar at once: Mayonnaise (Dijonnaise): The single best match for a sandwich spread. High in fat, neutral, and velvety, mayonnaise creates a classic Dijonnaise. A 50/50 or 2:1 ratio (mayo to mustard) retains the Dijon bite and creamy body while taking away the harsh nasal sting. Sour cream, crème fraîche, or Greek yogurt: A dollop folded into a spoonful makes a tangy, luxurious spread for roast beef or turkey sandwiches, as well as a base for cold sauces. Honey: Making a honey-dijon instantly cuts the perceived heat. Honey doesn't neutralize isothiocyanate chemically, but the concentrated sweetness overpowers the sensory sharpness on the tongue. Unsweetened applesauce or apple butter: A classic trick in European sausage condiments. Applesauce blends seamlessly into mustard, softening both the heat and acidity while maintaining a smooth spreadable texture. --- Method 2: Let Time and Air Do the Work Unlike hot pepper sauces, which can stay fiery indefinitely, homemade mustard naturally weakens over time. Refrigeration rest: Freshly made mustard is notoriously sharp during its first 48 to 72 hours. Stored in the fridge, the pungent enzymes naturally break down over 2 to 4 weeks, mellowing significantly on their own. Breathing at room temperature: Isothiocyanates evaporate. Leaving the jar open on the counter for a few hours (or leaving it out of the fridge for a day or two) will accelerate the dissipation of the volatile compounds. --- Method 3: Gentle Warmth (Cooking Applications) Isothiocyanates degrade rapidly when heated. If you prefer to keep the condiment in its pure jar form rather than diluting it, repurpose it for warm cooking instead of cold sandwiches. Stirring a tablespoon into a warm pan sauce (like a cream reduction for pork chops, chicken, or steak) will cook off the sharp nasal heat in under two minutes, leaving behind only the rich, savory Dijon flavor.

I think it's a simple as bad heat transfer often meaning uneven heat transfer, leading to burning. Burnt fond won't deglaze successfully. Compare deglazing with making a roux: in both cases you want the proteins and starches to be browned (by the Malliard reaction and caramelization) but not burnt. When making fond you want relatively high heat to promote these reactions and avoid the food (particularly some watery vegetables) from just sitting there in a lightly steaming puddle.

The key idea is that good heat transfer helps keep the pan surface at a more uniform, controllable temperature. Fond doesn't burn simply because the pan is too hot or because the heat is too low; it burns when the local rate of heat damage exceeds your ability to control it. There's also a small terminology issue: fond doesn't literally crystallise. The brown material left behind is a mixture of proteins, fats, and products of browning reactions, especially Maillard reactions. When you add wine, stock, or another liquid, those browned compounds dissolve or disperse into it, producing a glaze or the basis of a pan sauce. 1. What happens at the pan surface? Stage 1 — Browning The steak releases moisture. As the surface dries and heats up, Maillard reactions generate brown pigments and flavour compounds. Some of these compounds and residues adhere to the pan. Stage 2 — Fond formation The deposits accumulate on the hot metal. They continue reacting as heating proceeds, but they can also decompose, char, and become bitter if exposed to excessive temperatures for too long. Stage 3 — Deglazing Adding liquid cools the pan and dissolves or loosens many of the browned residues. These flavour compounds become part of the sauce rather than remaining stuck to the metal. The important distinction is that browning and burning are competing processes. Browning produces desirable flavour; continued thermal degradation eventually destroys it. 2. Why poor heat transfer can burn fond Imagine a thin stainless-steel pan heated by a gas burner. The flame doesn't heat the entire base uniformly. It creates hotter regions above the flame and cooler regions farther away. Stainless steel has relatively low thermal conductivity compared with copper or aluminium, so it spreads that heat sideways less effectively. The result can be substantial temperature differences across the cooking surface.  Conceptual temperature distribution Poor heat spreading Hot spots + cool spots Some patches scorch the fond while others are still browning. Good heat spreading More uniform heat More of the fond browns at a similar rate, giving you a wider window to stop cooking before it burns. Illustrations are examples of cookware, not measurements of actual pan temperatures. The mechanism is essentially a race between three processes: Formation: Heat drives browning reactions that generate desirable flavours and brown compounds. Degradation: Continued heating breaks down those compounds and eventually produces bitter, burnt residues. Heat redistribution: The pan conducts energy from hotter regions toward cooler regions, reducing local temperature differences. A poorly conducting pan redistributes heat less effectively. Consequently, a small region can accumulate enough thermal energy to burn its fond before the rest of the pan develops an adequate brown layer. 3. Then why do people say you need high heat? Because temperature and heat transfer are not the same thing. Temperature determines how favourable browning reactions are. Heat transfer rate determines how quickly energy reaches the food and how evenly it is distributed. Heat capacity determines how much energy the pan stores and how much its temperature changes when cold food is added. If the pan is too cool, meat releases moisture and may spend a long time steaming rather than browning. Evaporating that water consumes energy and holds the wet surface near the boiling point until much of the moisture is gone. Browning then accelerates as the surface dries and heats up.  But cranking the burner to maximum is not necessarily the answer. A pan with poor heat distribution can have a scorching hot spot even when the average pan temperature seems reasonable. The ideal is sufficiently high heat for rapid browning, combined with uniform heat distribution and enough control to stop before the fond burns. 4. Does the fond actually crystallise? Not in the ordinary chemical sense. The term may refer to the fond developing into a dry, brown, adherent layer as moisture evaporates and browning products accumulate. When you deglaze, water-based liquid dissolves or loosens many of those compounds. It doesn't reverse the burning process: if the fond has already charred, adding wine or stock won't restore its original flavour.  5. The practical takeaway For a steak and pan sauce: Preheat a suitable pan, but avoid letting it become excessively hot while empty. Dry the steak's surface and avoid overcrowding the pan. Let the fond develop from brown to deep brown, watching for black patches or acrid smoke. Adjust the burner as needed; don't assume maximum heat is best. Once the steak is removed, deglaze promptly with wine, stock, or water before the fond burns. One final nuance: high thermal conductivity is helpful, but it isn't the only factor. A pan's thickness, heat capacity, burner size, and heat-source pattern all matter. A heavy cast-iron pan, for example, can perform well because of its thermal mass even though cast iron conducts heat less effectively than copper.  iwww\.cookingforengineers.com+1 The central insight is that good heat transfer doesn't magically prevent fond from burning. It reduces temperature unevenness, while good heat management keeps the whole process within the useful browning window.

There are quite a few different strawberry cultivars. It'd be surprising if farmers didn't change which ones they plant in response to changing climatic and economic factors. Size and taste changes when they do that.

Mostly the strawberries, though a bit of both. Why store berries disappoint: Commercial varieties (mostly California-bred ones like Albion, Monterey, San Andreas) are selected for yield, firmness, and shelf life, not flavor. They're also often picked before full ripeness, since strawberries don't gain sugar after harvest. The fermented taste you describe is usually overripe or warm-stored fruit. Varieties to ask local farms about (Northeast June-bearers): Earliglow: widely regarded as one of the best-flavored; early season, sweet with real tartness Jewel: big, firm, classic balanced sweet-tart flavor Honeoye: reliable, bright flavor, though it can run tart Cavendish, Sparkle, Allstar, Mesabi: good flavor, though Sparkle and Allstar are less sweet-leaning Annapolis: early, good flavor Day-neutral/everbearing types (Albion, Seascape) are more hit-or-miss on flavor, so June-bearers are generally the safer bet. Picking tips: Go early in the season and early in the day, ideally a few sunny days after rain (heavy rain dilutes flavor). Pick berries red all the way to the shoulder, with no white or green near the cap. Smaller berries often taste better than giant ones. Skip anything dull, soft, or smelling winey. Ask the farm which varieties are in the field that week, since many will point you to their best rows. Eat at room temperature, as cold mutes flavor. If you tell me your state, I can look up farms and varieties near you.

You're good. Many people have fears about pork because of trichinosis, which has led to people overcooking port until it is dry and unpalatable. Trichinosis is extremely rare in most places, so you could eat it raw if you wanted to with very, very low chance of getting sick. Previously the USDA guidelines was to cook pork chops or roasts to 160°F (71°C), however there has been a recognition that this is overkill and it has been revised down to 145°F (63°C) as evidence has shown that temperature instantly makes the food safe. 154°F is far above what you need for safety. Your pork was a bit pink in the middle and still juicy, this is a good thing. Note: the guidelines for ground pork, beef and lamb are still to cook to 160°F (71°C).

Your Pork Roast Is Fine — Here's Why Short answer: You did almost everything right, and the roast is safe to eat. Let me break down what you saw. The pink center is normal (and not blood) Pink pork is expected, especially in the center, even at safe temperatures. The pink color comes from myoglobin, a muscle protein — not blood. It's the same reason cooked chicken thighs can look pinkish near the bone. Modern pork is leaner and often cooked to lower internal temps than the old "cook it to death" advice. USDA recommends 145°F with a 3-minute rest for whole cuts like roasts. You hit 154°F, which is above that. Pink juices are likewise just myoglobin-laced juices, not raw blood. Why it split at the center-line That's almost certainly the bone seam or the natural muscle separation in the roast. As the meat contracts during cooking, it opens along that line. It's cosmetic, not a sign of undercooking. The "crispy top" tells you the exterior got plenty of heat. One thing to double-check The only real safety question is whether your thermometer was accurate and read the true center. If it was an instant-read poked into the thickest part (not touching bone or fat), 154°F is solidly safe. If you're unsure, you can: Reheat the halves tomorrow to 165°F — that removes all doubt and is fine for leftovers anyway. Or just slice and eat cold; it's already cooked. For next time 145–150°F is the sweet spot for pork roast — juicier than 154°F. Pull it at ~140–142°F and let carryover take it to 145°F+. Rest 10–15 minutes before cutting (you did rest it — good). The split is normal; you can tie the roast with butcher's twine to keep it together if it bothers you. Bottom line Pink center + pink juices + a split along the seam = normal cooked pork, not a predicament. Your roast is safe, and wrapping it in foil in the fridge overnight is exactly the right move. Slice it thin tomorrow for sandwiches or reheat gently — you're good.

If you are interested in food safety alone, there is no problem. You might get a bit of a "starchy" or "floury" taste, but not necessarily so. The main ingredients are some kind of starch, sugar or other sweeteners, flavour and possibly some additives. None would pose a problem if eaten raw. But the real issue is that the texture of your dessert may be off: The main ingredient in an old-fashioned pudding mix is starch. That starch needs to be heated to gelatinize or, in other words, to thicken the liquid. To achieve good gelatinization, you need to boil the starch for a few minutes. For instant pudding, the starch is pre-treated and often other thickeners are included, so you can skip the cooking step. Depending in the recipe, using the type of pudding that needs to be cooked instead of instant, will likely result in a more liquid or soft dish. As you don't give the recipe you used, it's hard to say, how much it depends on the pudding for consistency, so you could end up with anything between a total failure and perfectly fine.

Yes, it is completely safe to eat. Uncooked "Cook & Serve" pudding mix contains standard, food-grade ingredients—primarily regular cornstarch, sugar, flavorings, and salt. There are no raw animal products (like raw eggs) or harmful bacteria in the dry mix that require cooking to become safe. While it poses no health hazard, the dessert's texture and flavor may be impacted: Texture: Cook & Serve pudding relies on heat to gelatinize regular cornstarch and thicken. Without that heat, only the instant pudding portion will properly set, meaning the mixture will likely end up softer, looser, or slightly runny. Mouthfeel and Taste: Because the cornstarch in the Cook & Serve mix wasn't cooked, you might notice a slightly powdery, gritty mouthfeel or a faint raw starch flavor. If the dessert is chilled and already layered (such as in a trifle or banana pudding), chilling it thoroughly in the refrigerator will help it firm up as much as possible.

If you can't get any pressure, it's something more than just the nozzle at the end of the tube ... it's something deeper in the mechanism (triggering the over-pressure release), or an issue with the gasket and threaded top. Try turning your sprayer over for a few seconds, then back right-side up and pump to pressurize the sprayer quickly about 2x more than your typically would, to intentionally over-pressurize it. Then listen for a hiss, and look for anywhere that might have bubbling or other signs of a leak. If it's in the gasket, you can try cranking down the plastic ring tighter, turning the gasket over, or replacing the gasket. If it's coming from somewhere else, you likely have to replace it.; they typically last 2-4 years (I've had some last longer, lots of people have reported failures after a few months, so read online reviews before picking a brand)

The problem is probably not just the nozzle. On a Misto oil sprayer, if the nozzle came off and now leaks and won't build pressure, the nozzle connection or the pump head's internal seal may be damaged. Here's how to troubleshoot it. How to fix your Misto 1\. Release all pressure Loosen the screw collar slowly to release any remaining pressure. Empty the bottle before inspecting the parts. 2\. Inspect the nozzle connection Check whether the nozzle stem is cracked, loose, or missing a small sealing piece. If the plastic retaining part has broken, pushing the nozzle back in may not create an airtight fit. Don't force it or glue it in place. 3\. Check the pump head and gasket Make sure the pump head is seated correctly and the screw collar is tightened securely. If air escapes around the cap or gasket, the sprayer won't build pressure even with a properly fitted nozzle. 4\. Replace the damaged part If the nozzle's retaining connection is broken, look for a compatible replacement spray head or pump assembly for your exact Misto model. The available instructions don't establish that the nozzle tip is sold separately. The manufacturer's instructions recommend filling the bottle only halfway and pumping until you feel resistance. If it never develops resistance, there is likely a pressure leak or a problem with the pump mechanism.  One thing I need to know Where exactly does the oil or air leak from? 1\. Leak location Around the small spray nozzle tip Where the nozzle stem connects to the pump head Around the large screw collar or bottle opening Not sure 2\. When you pump, what happens? The pump moves very easily, with no resistance The pump becomes hard, but oil still leaks The pump is stuck or cannot move properly Find the likely fault With those two details, I can narrow down whether you need a replacement nozzle, a seal, or the complete pump head.

The dotted line you see on Google Maps is the administrative border between the districts Yamakoshi and Abuta. Looking at other maps of the region, there is however a foot path from the station to the beach and to the Buddhist temple. If you look at Google Maps, there are several photo spheres along this path, and it seems easily walkable. I can find no foot path on the maps from the station to the nearby parking lot you are mentioning, but the distance is only about 400m and there are no obvious obstacles on the maps or on the aerial photos of the area, so I would assume that it is feasible to walk through the forest, even if there is no marked foot path there. On the Google Maps images from the station area, you can find a clearing in the forest in the right direction. The town of Toyoura has an information page about the nearby Buddhist temple, Iwayakannon. It says that the temple is accessible by boat or by foot from Koboro station. That seems to confirm, that there is at least no 'official' foot path from the station up to the road or parking lot.

Short answer: Not by car, but it is reachable on foot via unofficial trails. By car: The station has no road access, so "cannot be reached by car" is accurate. Atlas Obscura says it is almost inaccessible except by train or boat. On foot: A June 2023 YAMAP hiking log describes walking to the station from the Rebunge Pass side. The hiker crossed a stream on a log bridge on the way and urged extreme caution. That matches the dotted line you see near the highway on Google Maps. I could only find that one account, so I can't tell you how well-defined the path is. From the station onward: Footpaths lead to the Koboro cave (Iwaya Kannon) and the cliff-bound Buntaro beach. The trail down to the beach is described as steep, narrow, and largely unmaintained. The shoreline: I found no source confirming that walking along the coast to or from the station is feasible. Your doubts about the rocky shore seem reasonable, and there are sea-kayak maps of this coast, which suggests the water route is the more common one. Cautions: Don't walk on the tracks or through the tunnels, which is dangerous and not permitted. Before going, check current trail conditions with Toyoura Town (especially in snow season or for bear warnings), since I couldn't verify the trail's present state. Want me to look for the trailhead details near Rebunge Pass?

Here's what the national road traffic agency (Dutch: Rijksdienst voor het Wegverkeer) has to say: A tourist in the Netherlands? Are you not settling in the Netherlands, but you are here as a tourist? In that case, you can drive on the Dutch roads using your foreign driving licence.

Short answer No — your US driver's license alone is generally not sufficient, and yes — you should get an IDP, which you can obtain in the US (as a US license holder), even though you're an Indian citizen. But there are important caveats, and the rules differ slightly by country. --- 1. Do you need an IDP? Practically: yes, get one. Here's the breakdown for your three countries: | Country | US license alone? | IDP required/recommended? | |---|---|---| | Netherlands | A US license is accepted for short visits (up to 6 months) but it must be accompanied by an IDP if it's not in Dutch/English-friendly format. Dutch authorities officially state a US license is valid for up to 6 months, and an IDP is strongly recommended and often requested by rental companies/police. | Recommended / effectively expected | | Belgium | US license valid for up to 6 months for tourists, but Belgian rules require an IDP alongside a non-EU license (the license must be in a recognized language; an IDP resolves this). | Effectively required | | France | US license is valid for up to 1 year for visitors, but it must be accompanied by an IDP (or an official translation) because the US license is not in French. French law requires the IDP or a certified translation. | Required in practice | So for a round trip Amsterdam → Belgium → France → back, you should carry an IDP — it removes ambiguity at rental desks, police checks, and border stops. > ⚠️ Note: The above reflects general tourist rules. Rules can change, and enforcement varies. Always double-check with the relevant embassy/consulate or your rental company before travel. --- 2. Can an Indian citizen get an IDP in the US? Yes — this is the key point. An IDP is issued based on where your driver's license was issued, not your citizenship. Since you hold a valid US state driver's license, you apply for the IDP through the same US state agency (or AAA/AATA) that issues IDPs in your state. AAA and AATA are the two US entities authorized to issue IDPs, and they issue them to anyone holding a valid US license, regardless of nationality or passport. You'll typically need: your valid US license, a passport-style photo, a completed application, and a fee (~$20). You do NOT need to be a US citizen. Your Indian passport is fine. What you should NOT do: Apply for an IDP from India based on your Indian license (you'd need to be in India / use an agent, and it wouldn't match the license you'll actually present). The IDP must correspond to the license you carry — so get the US-issued IDP tied to your US license. --- 3. Practical checklist before you go Get the IDP from AAA/AATA in your US state (allow a few weeks; some offices issue same-day). Carry both together: your US license + the US-issued IDP. They're only valid as a pair. Check your US license validity covers your entire trip dates. Confirm with your rental company — many European rental agencies explicitly require the IDP for non-EU licenses. Carry your passport (Indian) as ID; some rentals/police may ask. Check current country rules via the Dutch RDW, Belgian SPF Mobility, and French ANTS/Sécurité Routière sites, or the respective embassies, since tourist-license rules can change. --- Bottom line US license alone: risky/insufficient for Netherlands, Belgium, and France as a visitor. Get a US-issued IDP (via AAA/AATA) — yes, you can, as an Indian citizen holding a US license. Carry US license + US IDP together for your Amsterdam–Belgium–France round trip. If you tell me which US state your license is from, I can point you to the exact issuing office/process for the IDP.

No, it will not make a difference. UK Standard Visitor visas are issued to individuals in their own right, and there is no legal requirement for him to enter the UK on the same flight or at the exact same time as you. As long as the core details of his trip match what he originally submitted in his application, entering alone will not invalidate his visa or cause problems at the border. --- Key Points for His Solo Arrival Be transparent if asked If the Border Force officer asks who he is travelling with, he should simply tell the truth: "I am visiting with my partner; she took a flight that routed via the US, but because I cannot transit through the US without a separate visa, I took a direct/alternative route and we are meeting at our accommodation." Border officials hear logical flight routing stories every day and will completely understand. Accommodation & Itinerary Details If hotel bookings, Airbnb reservations, or travel itineraries are in your name, make sure he has downloaded copies or printed confirmations on him. If the booking only lists your name, it helps if his name is either added to the reservation or he carries a copy showing your flight details confirming you are joining him. Proof of Funds & Return Ticket If his visa application relied on his own funds, he should be prepared to confirm his return flight date and how he is funding his stay. If you were declared as the sponsor funding his trip, he should have a copy of your bank statement and your flight itinerary proving you are arriving around the same time. eVisa / Vignette Verification Ensure his UKVI account and eVisa (or passport vignette) are active, and that he has access to his digital share code or travel documents on his phone in case an officer requests verification. As long as he has his accommodation details and return ticket ready, arriving a few hours apart on separate flights is standard and permitted.

Travelling internationally without any travel document is between very difficult and impossible depending on the details. If you need to leave the Schengen area and re-enter, you definitely need a passport. You would in all likelihood be refused boarding by the airline or blocked from leaving the Schengen area by the border guards. If you are travelling within the Schengen area and have a residence card, it might still be possible in practice even if it's not explicitly allowed. If you have nothing at all, you would probably still be able to physically cross the border but could get in serious trouble if you are found in another country with no document establishing your status. Even travelling in France is not without risk. Technically, you are supposed to be able to prove you are in France legally (i.e. show your visa) at any time if the police asks. If you don't have your passport on you, they could detain you for some time to check your status. Obviously, the requirement to surrender your passport for a visa application puts you in an awkward situation but there is no easy way around that.

Yes, you may be able to travel, but if the Spanish visa office keeps your passport, you generally cannot travel internationally without a valid travel document. As a Bangladeshi citizen applying for a Spanish visa while in France, the answer depends on where you want to travel and what documents you currently hold. Your situation Travel within France: You may be able to travel domestically without your passport in hand, but you should carry another accepted form of identification and proof of your lawful stay if possible. Travel to another Schengen country (such as Spain, Belgium, or Germany): You generally need a valid passport or other legally accepted travel document, as well as the right to travel under your current French immigration status. Travel outside the Schengen Area: This is much riskier while your passport is held. You may have difficulty boarding a flight or returning to France without the required documents. Importantly, submitting a Spanish visa application does not automatically cancel your existing French residence rights. However, if your current visa or residence permit is expiring, leaving France could create problems with re-entry. What I recommend Before submitting your passport, contact the Spanish visa centre or consulate handling your application in France and ask whether you can temporarily retrieve your passport. Some Spanish consular procedures allow passport withdrawal in emergencies, but you must confirm the policy for your specific application.  Useful official information: France-Visas — official visa guidance French government — returning to France after travel abroad Could you clarify one thing? Where do you want to travel while the Spanish visa office has your passport? A. Somewhere else in France B. Another Schengen country C. Outside the Schengen Area (for example, the UK or Bangladesh) Also, do you currently hold a valid French residence permit (titre de séjour) or a French visa? With those details, I can give you a more precise answer.

If you read the guidance, you will see that question 6.9 asks about "any criminal offence (including driving offences) in the UK or any other country, at any time?" while question 6.11 asks "Have you been subject to, or received, any other penalty by a court or the police; for example caution, discharge, fine or community sentence in the UK or any other country?" It seems clear that the answer to at least one these must be yes, and there is no exclusion for common traffic offences (on the contrary, they are specifically included). It is either a criminal offence or a "other penalty" and must be disclosed on your application. You don't know whether the UK authorities will be able to find out about this matter, but it's clear that they take even trivial omissions extremely seriously. Failure to disclose it will hurt your credibility and could lead not just to refusal now, but difficulty with future applications, even a 10-year ban for deception in the extreme case. As you note, it is a common traffic offence and rather unlikely to be cause for refusal. Failure to disclose it, when the form clearly requests that you do so, is cause for much worse. I would disclose.

Short answer: declare it. Sources differ on whether a minor fine like this is strictly required, but declaring is the safer choice. Your red-light fine is a penalty for a driving offence, and that's what the section asks about. The form's wording ("e.g. disqualification for speeding or no insurance") sounds serious, but it doesn't say minor penalties are excluded. Sources disagree on minor fixed penalties. Immigration lawyers say the form asks you to declare driving offences and fixed penalty notices. One firm says a minor offence dealt with by a fixed penalty notice, with no criminal record, is normally not required to be declared. That second view isn't a reliable basis to leave it out. Being refused for a minor fine you disclosed is unlikely. Commentary on UK applications says such fixed penalties must be disclosed even though they won't be taken into account when deciding. Note that most of these sources discuss citizenship or settlement applications, not visitor visas specifically, so treat them as guidance rather than the final word. The real risk is not disclosing. If the Home Office thinks you hid something relevant, it can treat that as deception, and that is far more damaging than one paid red-light fine. What to do: Tick "yes" and give brief, factual details: the offence, the date, the country, that it was a camera-detected fine paid in full, and that it never went to court. Keep the fine notice and your Australian confirmation that you have no criminal record, in case they're needed. If you want certainty, check the current GOV.UK visitor guidance or ask a UK immigration adviser. I'm not a lawyer, and the form wording can change.

Advance Parole is for people with certain pending applications in the US like Adjustment of Status or asylum, or certain statuses that cannot re-enter the US, like TPS, to leave the US and return to the US to resume the pending application or status. It doesn't apply to your situation. You might be able to get humanitarian parole, which is for someone outside the US who can't get a visa. Another option might be to contact the congressman or senator of your relative's district, and see if they can get your visa application expedited.

Can a German-Syrian Dual Citizen Obtain US Humanitarian Parole? Short answer Yes, it's legally possible — dual citizenship does not bar you from humanitarian parole — but it is discretionary, slow, and not a reliable solution for urgent travel. Given your facts, humanitarian parole is unlikely to solve your immediate problem faster than the visa process you're already in, and there are important caveats. Key points 1. Dual citizenship and the travel ban The March 2025 proclamation restricting entry for Syrian nationals applies to people who are outside the US and seeking entry as Syrian nationals. Having German citizenship does not automatically exempt you if you're also a Syrian national — but in practice, the visa/parole officer assesses your most recent nationality, passport used, residence, and ties. If you apply on your German passport and reside in Germany, you have a strong argument that the ban shouldn't apply to you. This is fact-specific and discretionary. The B1/B2 application you filed on your German passport is exactly the right posture — consular officers generally adjudicate on the passport presented, though they can consider all nationalities. 2. Humanitarian parole (I-131 / USCIS) Humanitarian parole is available for "urgent humanitarian reasons" — visiting a seriously ill relative can qualify. But: it requires a USCIS-approved I-131 with a sponsor (typically the relative or another US person), supporting evidence (medical records, doctor's letter), and payment of fees. Processing commonly takes months (often 3–12+ months), and approval rates are low and discretionary. It does not substitute for a visa and does not guarantee admission — CBP still decides at the port of entry. For a relative's illness, the more common path is expedited visa processing (see below), not parole. 3. The senator's involvement / "security clearance from Washington" This sounds like administrative processing (221(g)) or a security advisory opinion (SAO) on your visa case — very common for applicants with Syrian nationality, even when applying on a third-country passport. Consular officers cannot waive this; it runs through Washington. Senate casework can expedite inquiries but cannot override security checks. The timeline is genuinely unpredictable (weeks to many months). Keep the senator's office engaged and ask them to request a status update and, if eligible, an expedite. 4. Faster options to raise with the consulate/senator Expedited visa interview/appointment for urgent humanitarian travel (illness of a relative) — request via the consular section and the senator. Emergency appointment if the interview hasn't happened; expedite request if it has. If you're in Germany, you could ask whether another consular post has availability (though jurisdiction rules usually require applying where you reside). Keep evidence ready: doctor's letter detailing the illness and need for your presence, your relationship, and your ties to Germany (return intent). Bottom line Humanitarian parole: possible in theory, but slow and discretionary — not a realistic fix for urgent travel. Your best levers: expedite request on the pending B1/B2 + senator casework to push the security clearance, with strong medical evidence. Dual citizenship helps your argument that the Syrian travel ban shouldn't apply (German passport, German residence), but it does not eliminate security screening — which is what you're waiting on. Would you like a checklist of documents for an expedite request, or a template letter to the senator's office?

Yes, your situation makes perfect sense! You want to surprise your wife with a second week in Los Angeles after spending a week in Brazil, but you want to have a real airline ticket ready to show her. If she agrees, you go; if she can't go because of other commitments, you cancel the ticket and get your money back. Yes, this is possible. The key is to buy a ticket with a refundable fare or use an airline's cancellation policy that gives you a full refund. You do not necessarily have to pay for an expensive business-class ticket to do this. There are three options worth considering for a flight from São Paulo (or another Brazilian city) to Los Angeles. The three options 1. Buy a fully refundable ticket Best for your plan Buy a ticket for your wife from São Paulo (GRU) to Los Angeles (LAX) with the fare conditions explicitly stating that it is refundable to the original form of payment. You can then cancel it if she cannot go, even if several days have passed since purchase, provided you cancel before the applicable deadline and meet the fare rules. Important: A refundable fare may cost more, but it is the most suitable option for your one-week decision window. 2. Use the 24-hour cancellation window In certain circumstances, you can cancel for a full refund within 24 hours of booking. For tickets covered by the U.S. Department of Transportation's rule, the flight must be booked at least seven days before departure. The rule does not give you a full week to decide.  This is useful if you want to make a very last-minute decision, but it won't solve your situation if you need seven days. 3. Hold a reservation without paying Some airlines or travel agents can hold a fare temporarily without issuing a paid ticket. However, holds are generally short-term, and you shouldn't assume a reservation can be held for a week. This is worth asking about, but a refundable ticket is the more reliable approach for your plan.  US Department of Transportation Where I would start looking Two airline websites worth checking are: LATAM Airlines — Official cancellation and refund policy. LATAM explains that cancellation rights depend on the fare and where the ticket was purchased. For purchases in Brazil, its stated 24-hour purchase-cancellation policy applies subject to conditions; that is not the same as a seven-day refund guarantee.  American Airlines — Official reservations and tickets information. Its ordinary nonrefundable fares generally don't qualify for a refund after the initial 24-hour window, so look specifically for a refundable fare.  Whichever airline you choose, buy directly from the airline if possible. Before paying, confirm that cancellation after seven days returns the fare to your original payment method, rather than giving you airline credit or a voucher. One important detail for your surprise You don't need to print a boarding pass. Once you buy the ticket, you can print the booking confirmation or e-ticket receipt showing her name, the flight, the dates, and the reservation number. That is what you can present as your surprise. Before buying, make sure the fare is refundable after a full week, not merely changeable, and cancel it before departure if necessary. Dates not fixed yet Within the next 3 months I have specific dates Your preference for price Find the least expensive refundable option Any reasonably priced refundable fare Find suitable options The main thing is that you should be able to make your wife the offer with a genuine reservation, while keeping the option to recover your money if she can't go.

The "Working Holiday Program/Working Holiday Scheme" allows Australians (as well as Canadians and New Zealanders) under 31 years to stay in the Netherlands for up to one year. While this allows you to work, it's not mandatory if you have other means. This is basically the mirror image of similar programs in Australia, and the reason why the Dutch program is restricted to nationals of those countries.

There is no Schengen-wide long-stay visa, and the Netherlands has no visa for a long stay with no work or study purpose. These are the realistic options. 1. A national long-stay (D) visa from one country Long-stay visas are issued by one specific country and let you stay for more than 90 days only in that country. Italy's consulate says they are issued only for employment, study or residency purposes. Days on a national visa don't count toward your Schengen 90 days. Italy says Australians on one may also spend a further 90 days as tourists in the Schengen area before, during or after the visa. The category that fits you is a "residency on independent means" visa. I haven't verified current rules for these, so check the embassy sites. From memory, candidates are Spain (non-lucrative visa), Portugal (D7), France (long-stay visitor), Italy (elective residence) and Greece. Each requires proof of income or savings, health insurance and often a lease. This means basing yourself in that country, not in Amsterdam. Once you're resident there you can travel to the Netherlands as a visitor, but Dutch days will count against your Schengen allowance (check the rules in the country you choose). 2. Working holiday visa (if you're eligible by age) Several Schengen countries offer one to Australians, typically ages 18–30 or 18–35 depending on the country. Italy's allows a stay of up to 12 months, with limited temporary work. You don't have to work on it, but you must meet the age and funds requirements. I haven't confirmed whether the Netherlands has one for Australians, so check the Dutch IND site. 3. Study visa A course of 90+ days in a Schengen country qualifies you for a national study visa. Australians don't need a visa if the study programme is shorter than 90 days. A real course is required, not a token enrolment. 4. Bilateral visa-waiver agreements (older approach) Some Schengen countries have bilateral agreements with Australia. Examples are Denmark and Norway, which allow 90 days regardless of stays elsewhere in Schengen. Reports of the Germany agreement are similar. The source is about six years old and there's no confirmation that the agreements still apply, so verify with each embassy. Entry/exit tracking is also stricter now, and I haven't confirmed how it interacts with these agreements. Don't rely on this option without confirmation. Your UK/Ireland/Bulgaria idea This approach works. Time in non-Schengen countries doesn't count toward your 90 days. Bulgaria and Romania recently joined Schengen, so check their current status before relying on them. To narrow this down, how old are you? That decides whether a working holiday visa is open to you.

Okay, well let the soil dry out a bit more, but watering rules are these; water when the surface of the potting soil feels just about dry to the touch, but not so dry its shrunken from the sides of the pot; water well, and allow the excess to drain away freely from the base of the pot. Empty any outer pot or tray 30 minutes after watering, and again 30 minutes later if more has collected. The point of this is so the plant is not left sitting in water after it's taken up what it needs. The low temperature you have indoors is probably why its taken so long to dry out a bit, and maybe there was water in the tray when you watered it last. Note there is no need to push your fingers down into the pot to test the moisture content - just water when the surface feels a bit dry and let the plant drain down properly.

Monstera Soil Moist for 5-6 Weeks: Is This Normal? Short answer: No, that's not normal, and yes, you should be concerned. Soil staying moist that long is a recipe for root rot, even in winter. Why this is a red flag 5-6 weeks is far too long. A Monstera in a bright room should typically dry out enough to water every 10-14 days in winter, and more often in spring/summer. Even a slow-drying pot shouldn't stay moist for over a month. "Dry on top, wet below" is the classic signature of a compacted, poorly aerated mix or a pot that's too large for the root system — the top crumbles dry while the lower layers stay soggy because water can't move or evaporate. Wet little pellets deep down suggest the mix has broken down into dense, water-retaining material (often peat-heavy mixes do this over time). Once peat dries out completely it can also become hydrophobic, but here it sounds like the opposite — it's staying saturated. "Not saturated" isn't reassuring. Root rot doesn't require standing water — it requires prolonged moisture with low oxygen. Five weeks of damp soil is plenty. Likely causes Pot too big — your May photo shows a young plant; if it's still in that large pot with a small root system, the excess soil holds water for weeks. Dense/old soil — mixes degrade over 3-4 years, losing structure and drainage. Poor drainage — no drainage holes, or a cachepot holding water. Low light + cool temps + winter — slows transpiration. 12-15 ft from an east window is actually moderate-to-low light for a Monstera, which slows water use significantly. Overwatering habit — watering on a schedule rather than checking soil. What to do now Stop watering entirely until it dries substantially. Check for root rot: gently unpot and inspect roots. Healthy = firm, white/cream. Rot = mushy, brown, foul-smelling, sloughing off. Trim rotten roots with sterilized scissors. Repot into a smaller pot with a chunky, airy mix — e.g., potting soil + perlite + orchid bark (roughly 1:1:1). Terracotta or a pot with generous drainage holes helps. Improve airflow and light — move it closer to the window (a few feet from an east window is much better than 12-15 ft). Water only when the top 2-3 inches are dry, and always empty the saucer/cachepot. Consider a moisture meter if you're unsure — cheap and removes the guesswork. Bottom line A month-plus of moisture isn't winter dormancy — it's a drainage/aeration problem that's actively risking root rot. Unpot, inspect, and repot into a chunkier mix in a appropriately sized pot sooner rather than later. Waiting for spring is fine, but don't wait weeks — check the roots now.

The insertion point of the branch in the trunk will not move upwards, so you can leave it for few years and get apples next years, and only in few years you will create a branch above, or just prune it now and select a new branch.

The branch's joining point on the trunk will forever remain at its current height. It will never move upward as the tree grows. How Trees Grow Trees do not grow like humans or animals (where the entire body stretches uniformly). Instead, they grow via two distinct processes: Primary Growth (Length & Height): Vertical and outward lengthening happens exclusively at the tips of the shoots and branches, powered by regions of dividing cells called apical meristems. A tree gets taller by stacking new growth on top of existing wood, much like building a brick wall. Once a section of trunk forms, its vertical position is fixed permanently. Secondary Growth (Girth): Through the vascular cambium (a layer beneath the bark), the trunk and existing branches expand in diameter. Over the years, that branch union will become thicker, but its center point from the ground will never rise. What This Means for Your Tree Because that attachment point will remain 4 feet off the ground indefinitely, the branch will not naturally rise above your 5-foot wall. You have two primary options: Train the Branch Upward (Espalier technique): While the branch base cannot move, the flexible new growth at the branch tip can be redirected. Affix a bamboo cane or trellis wire to guide the branch diagonally upward until it clears the 5-foot mark, then train it horizontally over the wall. Apple branches are pliable during their first two seasons, making them well-suited for this. Prune and Wait for a Higher Shoot: If the branch is already too thick or rigid to bend upward safely, prune it back (either flush to the branch collar if unneeded, or to a lateral shoot that directs outward). As the central leader grows past the top of the wall, it will produce new buds at the exact 5-foot-plus height you want to send across the top.

You should look into hand pollination as well if the local pollinators are not cooperating. I had this same issue with my cucumbers and squash when I first started my garden. First, identify the male and female flowers. This is easiest to do by just looking under the base of the flower: Females will have what looks like a miniature squash or cucumber under the flower. Males will have a plain stem. Pick a male flower and expose the "anther" on the inside of the flower. Rub this gently to the center of the "stigma" on the inside of the female flowers. You can use one male flower for several females. You will be producing in no time, and hopefully from every female flower.

If your tomatoes grow well but your sweet peas, yard-long beans, and cucumbers grow lots of leaves and stems without producing anything to harvest, the problem is likely flowering or pollination, rather than your soil being completely unsuitable for vegetables. The key is to find out whether the plants are failing to produce flowers or whether flowers appear but don't develop into fruit or pods. Those are two different problems, and each has different solutions. Why this might be happening 1\. Tomatoes tolerate your growing conditions Tomatoes may be better suited to your garden's sunlight, temperature, and soil conditions than the other crops. Their success doesn't necessarily mean your soil has the right nutrient balance for every vegetable. 2\. Too much nitrogen fertilizer Excess nitrogen encourages leafy growth at the expense of flowering. If you use lots of manure, compost, lawn fertilizer, or high-nitrogen fertilizer, this could explain why the plants look healthy but don't produce. 3\. Poor pollination or flowers that don't set fruit Cucumbers usually produce separate male and female flowers. Male flowers won't develop into cucumbers; female flowers have a tiny cucumber-shaped swelling behind the petals. If pollination fails, the tiny cucumbers may yellow and fall off. 4\. Heat, watering, or insufficient sunlight Very hot weather, irregular watering, or too little direct sun can interfere with flowering and fruit set. This is particularly worth investigating for cucumbers and beans in a hot climate. What to check for each plant | Plant | What to look for | | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | Sweet peas | Flowers that drop, heat stress, or excessive nitrogen. If you mean edible peas rather than ornamental sweet peas, cool-season conditions are especially important. | | Yard-long beans | Whether flowers form and then fall off. Hot weather, dry soil, and excess nitrogen can all interfere with pod production. | | Cucumbers | Whether you have female flowers with tiny cucumbers behind them, and whether bees visit the flowers. | Heat can affect all three crops differently, and hot weather can reduce bean flowering and cucumber fruit set even when plants look vigorous.  What I would try first Stop adding high-nitrogen fertilizer for now, especially if the plants have very lush, dark-green leaves. Check sunlight. Aim for roughly 6–8 hours of direct sunlight daily for these fruiting crops. Keep the soil evenly moist. Avoid letting it dry out completely or leaving the roots waterlogged. Inspect the flowers. If cucumbers have both male and female flowers, try hand-pollinating a female flower with pollen from a male flower using a small, clean paintbrush. Consider the weather. If daytime temperatures are consistently above about 32°C (90°F), or nights stay very warm, heat stress may be a major factor. Bleach: It can be used safely, but it needs care. Plants: Bleach burns foliage and can damage roots if it pools in the soil. Risk is lower when diluted and kept off plants. Protect plants: Soak nearby plants and soil with plain water first, cover them with plastic or tarps, and rinse the deck and surroundings well afterward. Don't let runoff pool in beds. Personal safety: Wear gloves and eye protection. Never mix bleach with ammonia or acidic cleaners, since that releases toxic gas. Wood: Bleach can weaken and lighten wood fibers and corrode metal fasteners, so use the weakest solution that works and rinse thoroughly. Soap instead: Dish soap is much gentler on plants, though a heavy dose can still stress leaves, so the same pre-wetting and rinsing applies. However, soap only removes surface dirt. It won't kill mildew or mold or remove gray weathering, which matters before staining. Better middle option: An oxygen bleach (sodium percarbonate) deck cleaner cleans mildew and weathering with less plant and wood damage than chlorine bleach. If the wood is very gray, a wood brightener (oxalic acid) afterward helps the stain absorb evenly. Let the deck dry fully, usually 48 hours or more, before staining. If you tell me the plant types nearby and whether the deck is mostly dirty or mildewed, I can suggest a specific approach.

Mint in the Same Pot as Lime Trees Short answer You can physically put mint in the same pot, but it's generally not recommended for container citrus. The competition risk is real, and the containment benefit is largely an illusion in a pot. Why it's risky 1. Root competition is worse in a pot than in the ground Mint is a vigorous, shallow-rooted spreader that sends out runners aggressively. In a pot, the root volume is tiny and shared. Mint will colonize the soil surface and upper root zone fast, stealing water and nutrients that your lime needs — and citrus in containers is already on a tight water/nutrient budget. You'd likely see slower growth, more drought stress, and more frequent wilting of the lime. 2. Mint doesn't stay "contained" just because it's in a pot The containment argument works for bedding mint into the ground inside a bottomless bucket. In a shared pot, mint roots will interweave with the citrus roots. You can't easily separate them later, and repotting the lime becomes a nightmare. 3. Watering and feeding conflicts Citrus likes to dry down somewhat between waterings and needs steady feeding. Mint prefers consistently moist soil and also feeds heavily. Managing one pot for both is a compromise that suits neither. 4. Root disturbance when you repot Citrus in pots needs repotting every couple of years. Mint roots matted through the root ball make that job much harder and risk damaging the citrus roots. 5. Winter indoors Both overwinter indoors — that's fine — but mint may keep growing (or die back messily) while the citrus is semi-dormant, and the combined pot is heavier and harder to move. If you still want to try it Use a large pot (bigger than the lime alone would need) to reduce competition. Sink the mint in its own smaller inner pot (with drainage holes) plunged into the soil surface of the lime pot — this gives some root separation and makes removal easy. Refresh/divide the mint regularly. Keep the mint well trimmed and never let it flower/seed. Monitor the lime for signs of stress (yellowing, wilting, slow growth) and be ready to evict the mint. Better companions for potted lime If you want something in the same pot, choose shallow-rooted, modest, drought-tolerant plants that won't fight the citrus: Thyme or oregano (small, tough, shallow) Marigolds (annual, shallow, said to deter some pests) Nasturtium (annual, trailing, easy to pull) A living mulch of shallow annuals you replant each year Avoid: mint, lemon balm, chives/garlic chives (bulbous, spread), strawberries (runner-happy), and anything vigorous. For the runaway lawn mint The cleanest fix is to dig it out thoroughly (it will take repeated passes — every root fragment can resprout) and then either: keep mint only in its own dedicated pot (sunk into the ground with the rim above soil if you want it in the garden), or grow it in a bottomless bucket/section of pipe buried in the lawn, refilled with soil, so runners hit the barrier. Bottom line Put the mint in its own pot — not the lime's. A dedicated mint container contains it just as well (better, actually), and your limes will thank you. If you insist on co-planting, use an inner sunken pot for the mint and expect to manage competition actively.

While the concept seems straightforward, simply dumping river rock into a deep koi pond presents several serious safety and functional issues. However, you can convert it into a child-safe, temporary water feature that can be restored to a koi pond later if you take the right structural approach. --- The Problems with Just Adding River Rock Toddler Drowning Hazard: A 2-year-old can drown in as little as 1 to 2 inches of water. If a toddler slips on wet river rock and falls face down, they can become disoriented or trapped, making standing water—even at 2 inches—a significant hazard. Massive Structural Weight: Filling a standard koi pond (typically 3 to 5 feet deep) with solid stone requires several tons of rock. This immense weight can easily puncture, stretch, or tear the underlying EPDM liner, ruining it for future use. Removal Nightmare: Shoveling multiple tons of wet, algae-covered river rock out of a 4-foot pit in a few years is grueling, back-breaking manual labor. Water Stagnation & Pump Clogging: Solid rock drastically reduces water volume and traps leaves and debris between stones. This rotting organic matter turns into an anaerobic sludge pit, fouls your pumps, and creates putrid odors. --- The Better Alternative: A "Pondless" Feature with Water Storage Blocks Instead of filling the entire depth with stone, professional pond builders convert open basins into pondless water features using modular plastic crates (often called AquaBlox or water matrix blocks). How it works: Remove and Rehome the Koi: Safely rehome or board the fish. Protect the Liner: Lay an extra layer of thick non-woven geotextile underlayment across the bottom and sides to cushion the existing liner against abrasion. Install a Pump Vault & AquaBlox: Place a sturdy vertical pump vault at the lowest point (so your pumps remain easily accessible). Fill 80–90% of the pond's volume with structural AquaBlox crates. These hold massive structural weight while remaining 95% void space, storing the water reservoir needed to keep your fountains flowing continuously. Cap with Rock (Zero Standing Water): Cover the blocks with a layer of geotextile fabric, followed by 3 to 6 inches of decorative river rock or flat flagstone. Adjust the Water Level: Set the water level below the surface of the stones. The fountains will splash onto the rocks, vanish through the gravel into the underground matrix reservoir, and recirculate without leaving standing open water for a child to fall into. When you want the koi pond back: You simply pull off the top layer of gravel, lift out the lightweight plastic crates, and your deep, undamaged pond basin is immediately ready to be sanitized, refilled, and cycled for fish. --- Alternative Temporary Option: Heavy-Duty Safety Grating If you want to keep the pond fully functional with minimal effort, consider installing a sub-surface steel safety grate (such as PondSafety / SafaPond-style grates) or an above-ground perimeter mesh barrier. Rigid safety grids sit just beneath or at the water line, secured by tension bars, and can easily support an adult’s weight without restricting water flow or harming your equipment. However, because curious toddlers can drop toys or reach through mesh, a true pondless conversion remains the safest choice until your child is older.

Your suspicion is quite reasonable. A green, cross-hatched polytunnel cover could be reducing the light reaching your tomatoes, but the amount lost depends on the plastic itself, not just the reinforcing mesh. The combination of green tint, reinforced construction and a sheltered site could be significant. The commonly advertised figure of 90% light transmission for clear polytunnel film is plausible, but it isn't a universal figure. The important distinction is between: Light transmission: how much sunlight passes through the covering. Light diffusion: how much of that light is scattered rather than passing straight through. Spectral transmission: which wavelengths of light pass through. A green tint may change the balance of colours reaching the plants. The reinforcement grid may cause some additional shading, but the green plastic itself could be the bigger issue. So what percentage does cross-hatched covering transmit? I couldn't find a reliable, independently measured figure specifically for the cheap green, 1 cm-grid covers you describe. However, the available figures give us a useful comparison. Cover type Published light transmission Standard single-layer polyethylene film 85–87% Virginia Tech Clear horticultural polytunnel film Around 89–92% Clear Polythene+1 Reinforced PE mesh cover 80–85% for one commercial product specification Hangzhou Vitality Trading Co., Ltd. Your green, cross-hatched cover Unknown; no verified specification found The reinforced-cover figure is only an example, not a measurement of your particular cover. I wouldn't assume all reinforced covers transmit 80–85%, or that the mesh alone accounts for the difference. Are your tomatoes telling you something? Yes. Leggy growth is a recognised symptom of insufficient light, although excessive warmth and other growing conditions can contribute too. Your description raises two concerns: The green tint: it may reduce total light transmission or alter the light spectrum. Without the manufacturer's specifications, we can't quantify either effect. The surrounding buildings and fence: the tunnel may receive much less direct sunlight than its south-facing door suggests. The roof can be shaded for much of the day, even if the entrance is sunny. Changing the cover won't solve the problem completely if the site itself is heavily shaded. What I'd do in your position I'd lean towards replacing it with clear, UV-stabilised horticultural polythene designed for polytunnels, particularly if you intend to grow tomatoes regularly. Look for a published visible-light transmission figure of around 90% or higher, and check that the film is suitable for outdoor horticultural use rather than ordinary building or DIY plastic sheeting. Before buying, though, there's a simple test worth doing: On a bright day, compare the light immediately outside the tunnel with the light inside, at the same time and with the meter facing upwards. If possible, use a lux meter or a phone light-meter app. These aren't precision horticultural instruments, but they can give a rough comparison. Repeat at different times of day to see how much the fence and house contribute to the shading. Bear in mind that a phone's lux reading won't tell you the exact photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) reaching the plants, but a large, consistent difference between inside and outside would be informative. One question that would help narrow this down: is the cover a woven green mesh with a separate plastic coating, or is it a solid green plastic sheet with reinforcing threads embedded in it? That distinction could make quite a difference to the likely light loss.

Because the tree in question has the genetic potential to grow far taller than 8', and so in keeping it at that low height, you will essentially be pollarding the tree. You may not really like the result. It's normal for trees to grow tall and lanky before filling out. Usually, if people want them to look full and bushy as they grow, it is done by heading back (taking the last season's growth back, but not entirely removing it). This causes more branching, but also maintains proper proportions regarding to apical dominance, so you can maintain a healthy leader. If you cut the whole leader off, the plant's response the next season will be to put out a whole club of new leaders, which is not natural looking, or in the long run, structurally sound. So I would recommend heading back as possibly the heaviest pruning you should do, taking back up to 3/4 of all the new growth (if it is very long/whiplike), and then do similarly as the tree grows and matures. Just remember, the further you cut back, the more long shoots the cut end will throw out. For an '8 foot bonsai' look, I'd choose a tree with a maturing height in the 8' range.

Yes, you can keep it small, and pruning the leader won't harm it if you do it properly. Cutting the leader Prune in late winter, while dormant and before buds break. Cut back to a healthy side branch or a visible bud, not into bare wood. Larch can bud on older wood, but it's less reliable. The tree will usually grow a new leader from the buds near the cut. Pick the strongest one and remove competing shoots so you don't end up with a forked top. This also pushes growth into the sparse upper section, so it should thicken up. Holding it at about 8 ft Larch is naturally a very large, fast-growing tree, so this means regular maintenance every year, not a one-off cut. Each year, shorten the leader and the longest side shoots, and thin crowded growth. Light summer trimming of new shoots is fine. Avoid heavy cuts then. Don't remove more than about a third of the growth in one go. Spread bigger reductions over several years. Risks The main risk is cutting back to wood with no needles or buds, which may leave a dead stub. Larch is deciduous, so it tolerates pruning better than most evergreen conifers. It would also help to know whether it's in the ground or a container. A container makes size control easier because root restriction slows growth.

Short answer: No, don't use your cedar bark. Buy a proper orchid bark mix. While I appreciate the instinct to use what's on hand, cedar bark from your yard is a poor and potentially risky choice for a Phalaenopsis. Here's why, and what to do instead. Why cedar bark from your trees is a bad idea Fresh/raw bark isn't aged or composted. Orchid bark medium is bark that has been aged, graded, and often heat-treated. Fresh bark can contain resins, tannins, and other compounds that are phytotoxic or that throw off moisture and pH. Cedar is especially resinous. Cedar (and other aromatic woods) contain natural oils/resins that can harm orchid roots and are slow to break down in a way that's unpredictable in a pot. Particle size and consistency matter. Orchid bark is graded (fine/medium/coarse) so air and water move predictably through the pot. Hand-collected bark will be irregular—some pieces too big, some too small—which leads to uneven drying and root rot. Pest and pathogen risk. Yard bark can harbor insects, fungal spores, and mold. Commercial orchid bark is usually heat-treated/sterilized. It won't hold up the same way. Orchid bark is chosen partly for how it degrades over 1–2 years. Random cedar bark may break down too fast (soggy, suffocating roots) or too slow. So the "free materials" savings aren't worth risking the plant you're trying to save by repotting. What to buy instead A commercial orchid bark mix labeled for epiphytic orchids (Phalaenopsis). Medium grade is a good default for a standard phalaenopsis. Many mixes are "bark + perlite + charcoal" or similar—fine. Plain orchid bark is also fine. A small bag is cheap and will last through several repottings. Practical repotting notes Repot after blooms drop, as you planned—ideally when new roots are starting to grow. Soak the bark briefly before use so it's not bone-dry and hydrophobic. Use a pot with good drainage, sized just to fit the roots. Trim any mushy/hollow roots with sterilized scissors; keep firm, plump roots. Don't bury the crown—keep the base of the plant above the medium. Water less frequently right after repotting while roots recover. Bottom line Skip the cedar. The few dollars for a bag of proper orchid bark buys you consistent drainage, lower rot/pest risk, and a medium that behaves the way your phalaenopsis needs. Save the yard bark for mulch.
